prompt: What does each of NIST's four deployment models fix first?
hint: Location is allowed to vary in three of the four.

choices.text: Who the infrastructure is provisioned for
choices.why: Right. One organisation, a community, the general public, or a join of those: the tenancy comes first, and location and operator follow loosely.

choices.text: Whether the hardware stands inside the customer's building
choices.why: A private cloud may stand off premises and a community cloud on or off them. Location is what the models leave loose.

choices.text: How much of the stack the provider runs for the customer
choices.why: That is lesson 1's service model, IaaS, PaaS or SaaS. It is a separate question from who shares the hardware.

choices.text: Whether the service is billed per hour or by yearly contract
choices.why: Billing is not part of any deployment model; a private cloud with showback bills nobody at all.

prompt: A company rents a room of dedicated servers in a colocation facility and runs OpenStack on them, for its own teams only. Which deployment model is that?
hint: Ask who may run workloads on those servers.

choices.text: Public, because the building belongs to somebody else
choices.why: The building does not decide. Nobody outside the company runs on that hardware, so it is not open to the public.

choices.text: Private, standing off the company's premises
choices.why: Right. One organisation's workloads on dedicated hardware, and NIST lets a private cloud stand on or off premises.

choices.text: Community, since the facility also hosts other firms
choices.why: The other firms share the building, not these servers. A community cloud is one set of hardware for a group with shared concerns.

choices.text: Hybrid, because two companies are involved in it
choices.why: Two companies in a contract are not two clouds. Hybrid needs two distinct environments joined so a workload spans them.

prompt: Match each deployment model to who it is provisioned for.
hint: NIST's column 'provisioned for'.

pairs.right: One organisation and its business units
A group of organisations with shared concerns
Open use by the general public
Two or more distinct clouds, bound together

right_distractors: Whoever owns the building it stands in

prompt: Order these deployment models by who may run workloads on the same hardware, from the narrowest group to the widest.
hint: One organisation, then a group, then anybody.
trap: Community is not wider than public: its members have to qualify, while a public cloud takes anybody who signs up.

prompt: A colleague says: 'We sell SaaS, so by definition we are a public cloud.' What is wrong with the sentence?
hint: Lesson 1's question and this lesson's question are not the same question.

choices.text: Nothing: SaaS is always delivered from public infrastructure
choices.why: SaaS says how much of the stack the provider runs. It says nothing about who shares the hardware, and SaaS inside one organisation exists.

choices.text: SaaS is a deployment model, so it replaces the word public
choices.why: It is the other way round: SaaS is a service model. The two words answer two different questions.

choices.text: Service model and deployment model are independent questions
choices.why: Right. SaaS says what the provider runs for you; public says who shares the hardware. Any pairing is possible, so one does not imply the other.

choices.text: Public cloud covers IaaS and PaaS, not SaaS
choices.why: Public clouds sell all three service models. The error is linking the two axes at all.

prompt: Many customers' workloads running on one provider's shared hardware, kept apart by software, is called ___.
hint: A tenant is one customer.

prompt: The sheet's on-demand price for a t3.medium in sa-east-1 is 0.06720 USD an hour. What do 100 of them cost for one hour of load testing?
hint: The price is per machine and per hour.

prompt: Two customers' virtual machines run on the same physical host. What stops one of them from reading the other's memory?
hint: The first of the two layers of isolation.

choices.text: The firewall rules each customer writes
choices.why: Firewall rules filter network traffic between machines. Memory on the same host is not reached through the network.

choices.text: The API's identity check on each request
choices.why: That is the second layer, deciding who may create or change resources. It does not stand between two running guests.

choices.text: Nothing, which is why dedicated hosts are sold
choices.why: Dedicated hosts are for rules that forbid sharing, not because shared hosts have no boundary at all.

choices.text: The hypervisor, which keeps each guest apart
choices.why: Right. The hypervisor hands each guest its own memory, disks and interface and refuses a guest's attempt to reach another's.

prompt: A company's policy forbids running its workloads on physical servers shared with other companies, and it still wants a public provider's regions. What does the lesson offer it?
hint: Multi-tenancy is, in the end, a setting with a price.

choices.text: A larger instance type, which fills a whole server by itself
choices.why: Size does not promise a host to yourself. Only an option sold as dedicated makes that promise.

choices.text: Dedicated instances or hosts, sold at a higher price
choices.why: Right. The provider keeps that hardware for one customer, which turns multi-tenancy into something paid to switch off.

choices.text: Nothing: a public region means shared hardware, so it must build its own
choices.why: Providers sell dedicated options precisely for this rule. A datacentre of its own is one answer, not the only one.

choices.text: Encrypting its disks, which makes the host its own
choices.why: Encryption protects the data on a disk. It does not change who else runs on the same physical machine.

prompt: A datacentre runs its virtual machines on a hypervisor cluster, and a developer who needs one opens a ticket and waits two days. Which of lesson 1's characteristics is plainly missing?
hint: Who approves each machine?

choices.text: Resource pooling
choices.why: The hypervisor cluster already shares its hosts between teams. That is the one characteristic virtualisation did deliver.

choices.text: Broad network access
choices.why: The machines are reached over the company network, which is what that characteristic asks.

choices.text: On-demand self-service
choices.why: Right. A person approves and builds every machine; self-service means the developer gets one in minutes, with nobody approving it.

choices.text: Multi-tenancy across companies
choices.why: Not one of the five characteristics, and a private cloud has one organisation on its hardware by definition.

prompt: Which of these changes move that virtualised datacentre towards being a private cloud? Choose all that apply.
hint: Check each change against the five characteristics.

choices.text: A portal or API that creates a machine with nobody approving it
choices.why: Yes: that is on-demand self-service, the characteristic the ticket queue was missing.

choices.text: Moving the servers into a colocation facility
choices.why: Where the hardware stands changes nothing about the characteristics; NIST lets a private cloud stand on or off premises.

choices.text: Usage metered per team, even if nobody is billed
choices.why: Yes: that is measured service. Showback counts, with no bill attached.

choices.text: Letting other companies rent the spare capacity
choices.why: That changes who is on the hardware, towards community or public, and away from private.

prompt: Metering each team's usage and reporting it, without billing anybody for it, is called ___.
hint: The report shows; a chargeback bills.

prompt: A private cloud has 400 cores in its pool and the month-end batch asks for 600. Its automation is excellent. What happens?
hint: Elasticity inside a fixed pool.

choices.text: The extra 200 wait or are refused
choices.why: Right. Automation can hand out what the pool holds and nothing beyond it; more cores is a purchase measured in weeks.

choices.text: The portal sends the excess to a public region
choices.why: That is cloud bursting, and it exists only if somebody built the hybrid join. A private cloud on its own does not do it.

choices.text: Rapid elasticity adds 200 cores within minutes
choices.why: Elasticity in a private cloud moves inside the hardware it has. It cannot create cores that were never bought.

choices.text: All 600 run at full speed by sharing the 400
choices.why: Sharing 400 cores among 600 demands makes every job slower. Full speed for all is exactly what the pool cannot give.

prompt: What draws the line around who may use a community cloud?
hint: Not anybody, and not one organisation.

choices.text: Paying the provider's list price
choices.why: Paying is how anybody gets into a public cloud. A community cloud asks first whether you belong.

choices.text: Being located in the same city as the hardware
choices.why: Location is not the boundary; a community cloud can stand on or off its members' premises.

choices.text: Membership of a group with shared concerns
choices.why: Right. A mission, a regulator, a security requirement: the group defines the tenants, and an organisation has to qualify to join.

choices.text: Running every workload as SaaS
choices.why: The service model is a separate axis. Members of a community cloud can run IaaS on it.

prompt: A company keeps all its data in a region inside its own country, with a provider incorporated abroad, and concludes that no foreign court can ever order that data handed over. What is missing from the reasoning?
hint: Which of the sovereignty questions does a region answer?

choices.text: Nothing: the location of the disks decides which courts apply
choices.why: Location answers where the data is. The law of the provider's own country reaches it wherever its datacentres stand.

choices.text: Only encrypted data is protected by the choice of region
choices.why: Encryption is a separate question, about who holds the keys. The region choice by itself settles location and nothing more.

choices.text: The provider's home law reaches data it controls anywhere
choices.why: Right. The US CLOUD Act is the usual example: which courts can compel the provider depends on the legal entity, not the region.

choices.text: Regions inside a country are operated by that country's government
choices.why: Government regions exist, but an ordinary commercial region is run by the provider, under its own legal entity.

prompt: Match each sovereignty question to what answers it.
hint: A region answers only one of them.

pairs.left: Where are the machines and the data?
Which country's courts can compel the provider?
pairs.right: The legal entity that runs the service

pairs.left: Who may operate the service and reach the data?

prompt: An online shop's storefront runs in a public region and its stock database in the company's building. Order the path of one request for a product page, from the customer to the stock.
hint: The seam sits between the region and the building.
items: The storefront in the public region
The VPN tunnel over the internet
The ERP database in the company's building
trap: The VPN is not in front of the storefront: the customer reaches the region directly, and only the storefront's own lookup crosses the tunnel.

prompt: The office network and the new cloud network were both given the same private address range, and are now joined by a VPN. What goes wrong?
hint: Think like the router on each side.

choices.text: The traffic works, only more slowly through the tunnel
choices.why: Slowness is a separate matter. With the same range on both sides, a packet cannot be routed to the right side at all.

choices.text: Routers cannot tell which side an address is on
choices.why: Right. An address that exists on both sides is ambiguous, so the ranges have to be planned apart before the join.

choices.text: The VPN renumbers one side automatically
choices.why: A site-to-site VPN carries packets between the two networks; it does not renumber either of them.

choices.text: The provider refuses to create the tunnel at all
choices.why: The tunnel can be created; the trouble shows up as traffic that goes to the wrong place or nowhere.

prompt: Why is federation the usual answer for identity across a hybrid seam?
hint: Think about the day somebody leaves the company.

choices.text: Because a public cloud keeps no users of its own
choices.why: Public providers do keep users. Federation is chosen to avoid a second list, not because a list is impossible.

choices.text: Because the VPN only admits federated traffic
choices.why: The VPN carries packets; it has no opinion about how people sign in on the other side.

choices.text: Because federation encrypts what crosses the link
choices.why: Encryption on the link is the VPN's or TLS's job. Federation decides who somebody is.

choices.text: One directory says who everyone is
choices.why: Right. The cloud side trusts the company directory, so disabling an account there closes it on both sides at once.

prompt: A storefront in a public region asks the ERP on premises for the stock level on every product page. The VPN drops for twenty minutes. What happens, and what design would have kept selling?
hint: The seam is a dependency.

choices.text: Pages fail; a local stock copy and an order queue
choices.why: Right. With one crossing per request, the link takes the storefront down; periodic copies and a queue make the crossings few and asynchronous.

choices.text: Pages slow down; a faster dedicated link
choices.why: The pages do not slow down, they stop. A dedicated link fails less erratically, and it still fails; the design is what has to change.

choices.text: Nothing; the region is healthy, so the provider fails over
choices.why: The region is healthy and the storefront still cannot answer: its failure is joined to the link's, which the provider does not own.

choices.text: Pages fail; moving the ERP to a second provider
choices.why: A second provider adds a second seam. The problem is one synchronous crossing per page, wherever the ERP runs.

prompt: Which of these are hybrid arrangements in the lesson's sense? Choose all that apply.
hint: Hybrid starts when one workload spans both sides.

choices.text: A datacentre for payroll and a public account for the marketing site, never connected
choices.why: Two estates owned by one company are not hybrid until one workload needs both.

choices.text: A storefront in a public region that reads stock from the ERP in the building
choices.why: Yes: the storefront cannot do its job without the other side.

choices.text: Two virtual machines in two zones of one public region
choices.why: One provider, one region: that is a single public environment, whatever its zones.

choices.text: Production at home, with backups and a standby environment in a public region
choices.why: Yes: disaster recovery spans both sides, and the standby is useless without the copies crossing the seam.

prompt: Using the sheet's us-east-1 column, what does moving 50 TB out to the internet in one month cost?
hint: 51,200 GB: the first 10,240 at one price, the rest at the next.

prompt: What does sending 20 TB out of sa-east-1 to the internet in one month cost, at the sheet's prices?
hint: A TB on the list is 1,024 GB, and each tier prices only its own gigabytes.

prompt: An on-premises system uploads 50 TB from the internet into sa-east-1 in one month. What does the sheet charge for that transfer?
hint: Read the last line of the data-transfer block.

prompt: Somebody prices 50 TB out of sa-east-1 as 51,200 × 0.138 = 7,065.60 USD, since the month ends in the next-40-TB tier. What is wrong?
hint: Look at the offer file's ranges again.

choices.text: Nothing; the tier the month ends in prices the whole month
choices.why: That reading is the one the offer file rules out: each range carries its own price for its own gigabytes.

choices.text: The month should be priced at 0.150, the first tier
choices.why: Pricing everything at 0.150 gives 7,680.00, the other wrong shortcut. Only the first 10,240 GB pay 0.150.

choices.text: The first 10,240 GB pay 0.150; the rest pay 0.138
choices.why: Right. 1,536.00 + 5,652.48 = 7,188.48 USD: each tier prices only the gigabytes inside it.

choices.text: A TB is 1,000 GB, so it should be 50,000 × 0.138
choices.why: The offer's first range ends at 10240, so a TB on this list is 1,024 GB, and the tiers still apply.

prompt: The pull a large body of data exerts on the applications that use it, because moving it costs days and a bill per gigabyte, is called data ___.
hint: Like a mass that draws things towards it.

prompt: Order these ways of moving one GB from or into sa-east-1 by their price on the sheet, cheapest first.
hint: One of them is free, and one is the first internet tier.
items: To another zone of the same region
Out to the internet, beyond 150 TB in the month
Out to the internet, within the first 10 TB
trap: Leaving for another region is not free because it stays with the provider: from São Paulo it costs 0.1380 per GB, the same as the second internet tier.

prompt: A nightly job builds a 5 MB report from a 2 TB table. The table lives in sa-east-1; the report is read in the company's building. Where should the job run?
hint: Which direction is billed, and what is big?

choices.text: On premises, since data coming in costs nothing
choices.why: Coming in to the building is going out of the region: pulling 2 TB out every night is the billed direction.

choices.text: In the region, sending only the report
choices.why: Right. Compute goes where the data is; 5 MB crossing each night costs a fraction of a cent.

choices.text: Either side; transfer is priced per month, not per night
choices.why: The price is per GB, and 2 TB every night adds up across the month's tiers.

choices.text: Half on each side, to split the transfer cost
choices.why: Splitting the job still moves the large table's rows across the seam. Only the small result needs to cross.

prompt: Which of these is the weak reason for using two public providers at once?
hint: The one that sounds like free insurance.

choices.text: A managed service that only the second provider offers
choices.why: A good reason: the best tool for one job lives there, and the rest stays put.

choices.text: A large client's contract that names the provider it has to use
choices.why: A good reason: a customer's requirement is a real constraint, not a preference.

choices.text: An acquired company that already runs on the other one
choices.why: An honest reason, and a common origin: nobody designed it, and moving it has its own price.

choices.text: Failing over to the other provider by default, untested
choices.why: Right. It needs every part built twice, data copied at egress prices and failover practised; untested, it is a plan to find out during the outage.

prompt: A team wants its application to survive losing the São Paulo site of its cloud entirely. What does the lesson suggest before signing up with another company?
hint: One set of tools, one identity system, one bill.

choices.text: Nothing, since a region never fails as a whole
choices.why: Regions can fail, which is exactly why the team is asking. The lesson does not claim otherwise.

choices.text: A second region of the same provider
choices.why: Right. It covers the loss of one region with the tools the team already knows; a second provider adds only the whole-provider case, at a much larger price.

choices.text: A private cloud on premises as the standby
choices.why: That is a hybrid answer with a seam and a capacity ceiling of its own; it is not what the lesson puts first.

choices.text: A one-year commitment on all its machines
choices.why: A commitment lowers the price of machines. It does nothing for their survival when the region is lost.

prompt: An application built to run on two providers is limited to what both offer in compatible forms, which the lesson calls the lowest common ___.
hint: A term from fractions.

prompt: Does the LGPD require personal data about people in Brazil to be stored in Brazil?
hint: What does art. 33 regulate?

choices.text: Yes: art. 33 forbids keeping it on servers outside Brazil
choices.why: Art. 33 permits international transfer in the cases it lists. There is no general ban on storage abroad.

choices.text: No: the LGPD does not apply to cloud providers
choices.why: It applies to the processing, whoever's servers it runs on. The question is what it requires, not whether it applies.

choices.text: No: it regulates transfer abroad, in art. 33's cases
choices.why: Right. A transfer is lawful when it fits one of those cases, and the work is showing which one.

choices.text: Yes, unless every person has consented in writing
choices.why: Consent is one of the cases, and not the only one; and there is no rule that the data stay in Brazil to begin with.

prompt: Which of these is one of the cases in which art. 33 of the LGPD permits an international transfer?
hint: The forms of guarantee the article names.

choices.text: The destination region belongs to the same provider
choices.why: Staying with one provider is not a case in the article. What counts is the destination's protection or the guarantees offered.

choices.text: Guarantees given through standard contractual clauses
choices.why: Right. Standard contractual clauses are one of the named forms, and the ANPD published their text in 2024.

choices.text: Storing the data abroad is cheaper than storing it in Brazil
choices.why: Price is a reason to want the transfer; it is not a case that makes it lawful.

choices.text: The people concerned are customers rather than employees
choices.why: The article draws no line between customers and employees; both are data subjects.

prompt: A company's customer database runs in sa-east-1 and nowhere else. Which of these could still put customers' personal data in another country?
hint: Every copy is a location.

choices.text: A read replica in another zone of sa-east-1
choices.why: Every zone of sa-east-1 is in the São Paulo region. A second zone moves nothing out of the country.

choices.text: Staff in the São Paulo office querying the database
choices.why: Reading it from São Paulo keeps the data in Brazil.

choices.text: Encrypting the database's disks in sa-east-1
choices.why: Encryption changes who can read the bytes, not where they are.

choices.text: Application logs with customers' e-mail addresses, shipped to a monitoring service abroad
choices.why: Right. The database never moved, and a copy of personal data left anyway, through a tool nobody thought of as storage.

prompt: S3 Standard is 0.04050 USD per GB-month in sa-east-1 and 0.02300 in us-east-1. How much more a month does keeping 1,000 GB in sa-east-1 cost?
hint: The difference per GB, times the gigabytes.

prompt: For an m7i.large in sa-east-1, the sheet gives 0.16065 USD an hour on demand and 0.09956 on a 1-year reservation with no upfront payment. Over a 730-hour month, how much does the reservation save?
hint: The difference per hour, times 730.

prompt: Which of these workloads is the strongest candidate for moving back to owned hardware?
hint: The shape of the load, and who would run it.

choices.text: A storefront whose traffic multiplies on Black Friday
choices.why: A spike is what rented capacity is for; owned hardware would be sized for that one week and idle for the rest.

choices.text: A large steady system, busy around the clock for years, run by a team that operates hardware
choices.why: Right. Steady load leaves little idle margin, and the team already covers the people cost the spreadsheet forgets.

choices.text: A new product whose usage doubles every quarter
choices.why: Fast growth is a capacity-planning bet you would lose either way: buy too little and run short, buy too much and pay for idle metal.

choices.text: An application built on three managed services
choices.why: Leaving means rebuilding and running those services yourself, a cost the purchase price of a server never shows.

prompt: Match each cost that a repatriation spreadsheet forgets to what it is.
hint: None of them is on the server's invoice.

pairs.right: Somebody on call when a disk fails at three in the morning
Power, cooling and space, or colocation fees
Replacing the hardware every few years
Buying ahead for the peak, plus growth, plus a spare

right_distractors: A price per request to the provider's API

prompt: A spreadsheet compares the purchase price of three servers with a year of on-demand bills for the same machines and concludes that buying saves money. Which correction comes first?
hint: Both columns are wrong, in opposite directions.

choices.text: Use the committed price, and add people, building and refresh
choices.why: Right. The cloud column is too high, since a commitment takes off about a third, and the owned column is too low, since the servers are the cheapest part.

choices.text: Leave it; the purchase price is the whole cost
choices.why: The purchase price leaves out the people, the building and the next refresh, which is why the spreadsheet looks so easy.

choices.text: Price the cloud side with a bigger instance type
choices.why: Changing the machine changes the question. The error is which price and which costs, not which instance.

choices.text: Add a month of egress to the cloud column
choices.why: Egress belongs to the move and to heavy traffic, and it counts; but it does not fix a comparison against the wrong price.

prompt: Match each trait of a workload to where the lesson's table says it pushes.
hint: Each row of the table has a 'because'.

pairs.right: Public, renting the peak only while it lasts

pairs.left: Tight latency to machines on the shop floor
pairs.right: That part kept on premises, hybrid for the rest

pairs.left: A rule that forbids shared hardware
A very large dataset already in one place

right_distractors: Two providers at once, by default

prompt: A research lab runs a genome pipeline twice a year for three weeks, needing 2,000 cores; the rest of the year it needs about 50. It owns a 64-core cluster. Which arrangement fits?
hint: Two traits: a small steady part and a rare, large peak.

choices.text: Buy 2,000 cores so the pipeline never waits
choices.why: Those cores would sit idle for about forty-six weeks a year; idle capacity is the price of control, paid whether used or not.

choices.text: A one-year commitment on 2,000 cores in a public region, for a lower price
choices.why: A commitment pays for the machines all year; it suits steady load, which the peak is not.

choices.text: The cluster for the steady part, a public region for the peak
choices.why: Right. The small steady load fits what the lab owns, and the rare peak is exactly what rented capacity is for.

choices.text: Split the pipeline across two public providers
choices.why: Nothing in the traits calls for a second provider; it would add two identity systems and two bills to a lab.

prompt: Why does the lesson say 'should our company be public, private or hybrid?' has no good answer?
hint: What do the models actually describe?

choices.text: Hybrid is always the right answer for a company
choices.why: Hybrid is the result for some sets of systems, like the shop's, and none at all for a company whose systems never meet.

choices.text: A model describes one system; a company has several
choices.why: Right. The question is asked per system, from its traits, and the answer is one word per system, joined where they meet.

choices.text: Only the provider can decide which model applies
choices.why: The provider sells capacity; which system goes where is the customer's decision, argued from the traits.

choices.text: The models are marketing words with no definition
choices.why: They have definitions, NIST's, and the lesson uses them. Sovereign is the label without one.

prompt: Two environments joined so that one workload spans them, such as a public storefront reading an on-premises ERP, are called a ___ cloud.
hint: NIST's fourth model.

prompt: An online bookshop in Recife wants to keep its customer records in us-east-1, because the sheet's prices are lower there. Which statement is right?
hint: Transfer, not localisation.

choices.text: It cannot: the LGPD requires the records to stay in Brazil
choices.why: The LGPD has no general localisation rule. It regulates transfer abroad and lists when it is permitted.

choices.text: It can, with no further thought: the provider answers for the LGPD
choices.why: The bookshop is the controller of its customers' data. The provider does not take that over.

choices.text: It can if the transfer fits a case in art. 33
choices.why: Right. The lower price is a reason to want it; one of the listed cases is what makes it lawful.

choices.text: It can once the records are encrypted, since that removes the transfer
choices.why: Encrypted personal data sent abroad is still data sent abroad. Encryption answers a different question.

prompt: A video service sends 60 TB a month out of sa-east-1 to the internet. What does that month's transfer cost at the sheet's prices?
hint: Three tiers this time.

prompt: Each month an on-premises system sends 5 TB up into sa-east-1 over a VPN and fetches 5 TB back. Which of the two directions does the sheet charge?
hint: Which side of the seam is the provider's?

choices.text: Both, at the same price per GB
choices.why: The two directions are priced differently: in from the internet is 0.0000.

choices.text: Only the upload into the region
choices.why: The upload is data coming in, which the sheet prices at zero.

choices.text: Neither, because a VPN is a private connection
choices.why: The VPN travels over the internet, and data leaving the region through it is billed as data out.

choices.text: Only the 5 TB fetched back out of the region
choices.why: Right. Out of the region is billed per GB, 5 TB within the first tier at 0.150; in from the internet costs nothing.
